contract: fuzz(target) -> list of str. target = {'subject': str, 'entry': str (how one input is executed), 'files': {path: source} (the subject's CPython 3.12.14 files as the evaluator loads them), 'instrumented': [paths whose coverage counts], 'max_inputs': 1000, 'max_chars': 2000}. Return at most max_inputs strings of at most max_chars characters. The evaluator imports the files under a private package name, inserts a numbered probe at the start of every block inside the functions of the instrumented files (function entry; if and else branches, including an empty else; loop bodies and normal loop exits; try bodies, else and finally blocks; exception handlers; with bodies; match cases; both branches of conditional expressions), runs the entry on every input (exceptions are expected and ignored; 0.5 s of CPU time per input) and counts the distinct probes reached. Entries: tomllib -> tomllib.loads(text); re -> re._compiler.compile(text, 0), i.e. regular-expression parsing and compilation; html.parser -> for convert_charrefs in (True, False): HTMLParser(convert_charrefs).feed(text) then close(); plistlib -> plistlib.loads(text.encode('latin-1')), so each character U+0000-U+00FF is one byte and the XML or binary format is detected from the bytes (characters above U+00FF only raise the encoding error). Score: number of distinct probes reached, maximised; replaying all inputs may take at most 120 s of CPU time, otherwise the evaluation is invalid. fuzz() runs in a sandboxed subprocess (no files, network or subprocesses; 60 s CPU, 2 GB) and may load and run the given files itself, for example to trace coverage; it should be deterministic (seed any randomness, do not read clocks).
notes: Targets are pure-Python CPython 3.12.14 modules (PSF licence) imported from source under a private package name; html/parser.py is patched to import that copy of _markupbase. Coverage is counted with the evaluator's own block probes (no coverage.py), and the corpus is bounded by size instead of the wall-clock budgets of fuzzing benchmarks; probe counts depend on these sources, not on the interpreter's line events.

name: Software engineering: coverage-guided fuzzing of CPython's tomllib
description: Generate at most 1,000 input strings that drive the TOML parser tomllib (CPython 3.12.14) through as many code blocks as possible. The score is the number of distinct instrumented blocks (function entries, branch outcomes, loop exits, handlers) that the inputs reach.
benchmark: Software engineering: coverage-guided fuzzing of CPython's tomllib
paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

sources.locator: Bohme, Pham and Roychoudhury (CCS 2016): coverage-based greybox fuzzing, where reaching new coverage guides input generation.
Godefroid, Kiezun and Levin (PLDI 2008): grammar-based fuzzing of parsers to reach code beyond the lexer.
Klees, Ruef, Cooper, Wei and Hicks (CCS 2018): how fuzzers are evaluated, including coverage as a measure.
CPython 3.12.14 source release (PSF licence): the pure-Python target modules and the test inputs used as references.

limitations: Coverage is a proxy: no faults are seeded and crashes are not scored, while fuzzing research also measures bugs found (Klees et al. 2018).
Block probes are this evaluator's own instrumentation of the pinned sources (no coverage.py or compiler edges), so counts are not comparable with other coverage tools; some probes are unreachable.
The corpus is bounded by size (1,000 strings of at most 2,000 characters) and generation by 60 s of CPU time instead of the hours-long wall-clock budgets of fuzzing benchmarks.
Reference computed here: the 62 TOML files of CPython's tomllib test data reach 278 of the 305 probes; the random-string seed reaches fewer.
The target is pure Python executed by CPython; results say nothing about memory-safety bugs in C code.

science_relevance.scientific_problem: Automated test input generation (fuzzing) for parsers: produce inputs that exercise as much of a parser's logic as possible, since unexercised code cannot reveal its faults.
science_relevance.importance_rationale: Parsers process untrusted input and are a main source of security and robustness defects; coverage-guided and grammar-aware fuzzing are among the most widely used and studied testing techniques.

papers.title: Coverage-based Greybox Fuzzing as Markov Chain
papers.primary_goal: Make coverage-guided greybox fuzzing reach more program paths with the same number of executions.
papers.task_relation: The task rewards inputs by the program coverage they reach.

papers.title: Grammar-based whitebox fuzzing

papers.task_relation: The targets are parsers, where input structure decides which code is reached.
